purpose: One set of examples for the two implementations of the test that finds the picture in a card's named picture field (cached_image, image, image_url and the others), so a change to one side that the other does not follow fails a test instead of showing a card and its article two different pictures.
note: Each input is a field's raw text and each picture is the browser's answer for it, an empty text meaning no picture. Two cases cannot be listed: a JSON escape of a lone UTF-16 surrogate, which a Go string cannot hold, and nesting thousands of levels deep, where each side stops at a limit of its own.

examples.why: A stored file name is a picture.
Surrounding spaces are trimmed off.
So is a row-scoped logo's stored name.
The stored-name pattern accepts any extension.
A storage path needs no extension.
A storage path may name a size folder.
A rooted path is a picture.
An https address is a picture even without an extension.
So is an http address.
So is a path relative to the page.
So is a path to a parent folder.
An extension in capitals, followed by a query.
An extension followed by a fragment.
An empty field holds no picture.
Nor does white space alone.
The text null, seen in a live database, is no picture.
A plain word is no picture.
An extension must end the text.
An extension that is part of a longer word does not count.
A path whose third part is neither a number nor original is no storage path.
A stored name needs its extension.
The text of a number is never a picture.
A JSON array as the whole text is not read; only an object is.
Text that opens an object without closing it is not read.
Braces around text that is not JSON hold nothing.
The first value that holds a picture wins.
An empty value is passed over.
So is a value that holds no picture.
Names that are array indexes come first, in ascending order.
Index names come before all other names, wherever they are written.
A number written with a leading zero is an ordinary name and keeps its written place.
2^32-1 is no array index, so it keeps its written place.
2^32-2 is the largest array index and comes first.
A repeated name keeps its last value.
A repeated name keeps its first place and its last value.
Two objects in one text: JSON.parse reads one whole value only.
Nor may any other text follow the object.
A nested object is searched in its turn.
JSON.parse keeps __proto__ as an ordinary name.
Escapes are read as JSON.parse reads them.
JSON white space may surround names and values.
A no-break space is not JSON white space, so JSON.parse fails.
A JSON object inside a string value is read in its turn.
An unreadable object inside a string holds nothing, and the search goes on.
An empty object holds nothing.
Numbers, truth values and null hold no picture.
The search passes over them.
An own toString does not matter to an object that is searched, not turned into text.
An array is read as its elements joined by commas.
The whole joined text is the picture.
The joined text is trimmed.
A nested array is joined the same way.
null joins as nothing.
A trailing null leaves a comma after the extension.
An empty array and an array of null join as nothing.
Truth values join as true and false.
An object joins as [object Object].
A number joins as JavaScript writes it: 1e21 in exponent form.
Plain numbers keep their shortest form; -0 is written 0.
Exponent form from 1e21 up and below 1e-6.
The shortest digits that read back as the same double.
Beyond the double range a number is infinite, or zero.
The joined text is tested in full: this one opens like an address.
An empty array joins as nothing, and the search goes on.
A number alone joins into text that is no picture.
The joined text is read as JSON again, under a try of its own.
Elements joined by their comma can form one object.
Joined text that cannot be read holds nothing, and the search goes on.
Joining it throws, and the throw ends the search of the whole text.
The throw also takes the array's own picture with it.
Inside a nested array as well.
An escaped name is still toString.
A picture found before the throwing value wins.
Index names come first, so the picture is found before the throw.
A throw inside an object encoded in a string ends only that string's search.
So does a throw inside the text an array joins into.
An own valueOf does not stop the join.
Only the element's own toString matters, not a nested one.
Tabs, line ends, vertical tabs and form feeds are trimmed.
So are the Unicode space separators.
So are the line and paragraph separators.
So is a byte order mark, which Go's TrimSpace keeps.
U+0085 is not trimmed, though Go's TrimSpace removes it; the name then no longer ends with its extension.
U+180E is no longer white space: it stays, and the extension still makes a picture.
A value inside JSON is trimmed the same way.
So is one whose spaces are written as JSON escapes.
JavaScript's . does not match a line feed.
Nor a carriage return, which Go's . matches.
Nor a line separator.
Nor a paragraph separator.
U+0085 is no line terminator, so . matches it.
A storage path cannot run over a line end.
Nor over a line separator.
The long s is no s: the /i flag folds only ASCII letters here, where Go's (?i) folds it.
ASCII capitals match.
